question: Attacks on ships by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have led to ships being routed around the southern tip of Africa rather than taking the shorter route through the Suez Canal. This has raised shipping costs. Has the Commission estimated what impact this will have on inflation in 2024? If so, what impact will it have? If not, why not?
answer: The Winter interim Forecast 2024 (1) includes a box analysing the impact of the Red Sea crisis, including on inflation. The Commission updated its assessment as part of the Spring Forecast 2024 (2). Escalating tensions in the Middle East continue to lead to diversion of trade, though with so far only limited impact on supply chains and prices.

The number of ships going through the Red Sea in mid-March 2024 was around half that at the end of 2023, while the number of ships going around the Cape of Good Hope tripled. The number of ships docking at northern European ports fell by around 25% in December 2023 and January 2024 compared to the weekly average for 2023, but by mid-February this gap had reduced to 15%.
Shipping rates rose in early 2024 to almost double their average 2023 level but fell back by around 20% from mid-February to mid-April 2024. They remain well below the peaks of late 2021.

The continued deceleration in producer prices in the goods manufacturing sectors provides evidence for the absence of a tangible pass-through from shipping disruptions in the Red Sea, amid relatively weak economic momentum and over-capacity in the transport industry.
